blindSummary:
This is a high-risk destination for trans visitors — one of only five countries in its region still criminalising same-sex conduct (buggery carries life imprisonment on paper, though rarely enforced). In November 2024 a regional human-rights commission heard evidence of severe violence against trans women: 69 cases of violence against trans women documented 2018-2022, in a country of under a million people. Police fail to investigate anti-LGBT violence; there is no anti-discrimination legislation (a UN human-rights committee called for one in April 2024) and no legal gender recognition.

Cross-dressing was decriminalised after a 2018 ruling of a regional court of final appeal, brought by trans women claimants, removing the most direct trans-expression statute, but the climate and investigative failure keep risk high. The capital has a small organised community served by a local LGBT advocacy organisation.
blindOutOfScope: Buggery statutes are rarely enforced (climate/situational); a regional court of final appeal struck the cross-dressing laws in 2018.
blindTangential: Buggery (life imprisonment on paper, rarely enforced) remains a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2018 ruling of a regional court of final appeal struck the cross-dressing laws.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): this is one of only five countries in its region still criminalising consensual same-sex conduct - criminal-law provisions covering 'gross indecency', attempted buggery and buggery with life imprisonment. Rarely enforced but fuels stigma. In 2025 five of six election-contesting parties, including the ruling party, supported decriminalisation. Cross-dressing was criminalised until 2018 under a catch-all provision of a colonial summary-jurisdiction statute, targeting trans people; no legal gender recognition.

Regional human-rights commission hearing record (2024 session): civil-society hearing on LGBTI rights and gender-based violence in this country - part of the commission's special-rapporteur mechanism for LGBTI persons.

National news outlet (Nov 2024): at a regional human-rights commission hearing requested by a local group, testimonies on gender-based violence in this country were heard; the commission called on the state to take urgent action.

Foreign public broadcaster (March 2017): transgender activists in this country fight an 1893 colonial-era cross-dressing law (a catch-all summary-jurisdiction provision); a trans woman activist was stabbed and attacked with bottles, then told by the magistrate to 'dress like a man' - 'we live in a very homophobic society.'

National news outlet (Nov 2018): a regional court of final appeal ruled in favour of transgender women claimants - the cross-dressing law is unconstitutionally vague and violates freedom of expression; the colonial-era provision was struck from the statute book.

LGBTQ news outlet (March 2017): transgender activists in this country fight archaic transphobic laws - the scissors attack on an activist, the magistrate ordering her to 'dress like a man', and the 124-year-old cross-dressing law blocking justice.

National TV news channel (May 2019): the head of a local LGBT organisation documents police using discriminatory laws to extort LGBT persons - men in 'compromising positions' threatened with arrest to extract bribes; those who do report face further discrimination at police stations.
